Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verses 9–14:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Who made the earth for you as a cradle﴾, meaning a bed (firash).

﴿And made for you therein roads﴾, meaning paths (turuq).

It may also carry a second meaning: means of livelihood (ma'ayish).

﴿So that you may be guided﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

One: that you may be guided on your journeys. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The second: that you may recognise God's blessing upon you. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

It may also carry a third meaning: that you may be guided to your livelihoods.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And Who created all the pairs﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

The first: all kinds (asnaf). This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: the pairs of animals, male and female. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: that the pairs are winter and summer, night and day, the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon, Paradise and the Fire. This was said by al-Hasan.

It may also carry a fourth meaning: that the pairs are what people experience of good and evil, faith and disbelief, wealth and poverty, health and sickness.

﴿And made for you of the ships﴾, meaning the ships (sufun).

﴿And of the cattle that you ride﴾. Regarding "cattle" here there are two views:

One: camels and cattle. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second: camels alone. This was said by Mu'adh.

Thus He reminded them of His blessings upon them in their travelling by land and by sea.

Then He said: ﴿That you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. He attributed the backs (al-zuhur) to a singular noun because what is meant by it is the genus (al-jins), so the singular became equivalent in meaning to the plural.

﴿Then you may remember the blessing of your Lord when you are settled upon them﴾, meaning when you have mounted them.

﴿And say: Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾, meaning who has made this mount tame for us.

﴿And we were not capable of it﴾. Regarding this there are three views:

The first: controlling them (dabitin). This was said by al-Akhfash.

The second: matching them in strength and power. This was said by Qatada, from their saying "he is the qarn of so-and-so" when he is his equal in strength.

The third: being able to manage them (mutiqin). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi. Qutrub recited a line of verse by 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

Indeed the tribes know that 'Aqil, for us, in calamities, are not our equals (muqrinin).

As for its root, there are two views:

One: that its root is taken from iqran, as one says "so-and-so aqran" when he was able.

The second: that its root is taken from muqarana (pairing), which is that some of them are paired with others in travel.

Sulayman ibn Yasar related that a group of people were on a journey, and whenever they mounted they would say: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we were not capable of it﴾. Among them was a man on a she-camel of his that was emaciated, so that it did not move from thinness. He said: "As for me, I am able to manage this one." She then broke with him and crushed his neck.

It may also carry a fourth meaning: that the pairs are what people experience of good and evil, faith and disbelief, wealth and poverty, health and sickness.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verse 15–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they have attributed to Him from among His servants a portion﴾. In it there are four interpretations:

The first: equal, i.e., a likeness. This is related from Qatadah.

The second: offspring from the angels. This is related from Mujahid.

The third: a share. This is related from Qutrub.

The fourth: that it means daughters. In the view of the people of Arabic linguistics (ahl al-'arabiyyah), al-juz' (portion) means daughters.

It is said: "The woman has given birth to a portion (ajza'at al-mar'ah)" when she bears daughters.

The poet said:

"If she has borne a people a portion once, there is no wonder; the free woman sometimes bears a male as well."

﴿Indeed, man is ungrateful﴾. Al-Hasan said: he counts the calamities and forgets the blessings.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, i.e., of that which they assigned to the Most Merciful: daughters, and to themselves: sons.

﴿His face becomes darkened﴾ admits of two interpretations:

The first: by the invalidity of the likeness that he set forth.

The second: by what he was given good news of, namely the female.

﴿And he is inwardly distressed﴾. In it there are three interpretations:

The first: sorrowful. This is related from Qatadah.

The second: grieved. This is related from Ikrimah.

The third: silent. This is related by Ibn Abi Hatim.

This is due to the corruption of his likeness and the invalidity of his argument.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Is one who is brought up in ornament...﴾. Al-nushu' is upbringing, and al-hilyah is adornment.

Regarding what is meant by it, there are three interpretations:

The first: the female slaves (al-jawari). This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: the daughters. This is related from Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: the idols. This is related from Ibn Zayd.

Regarding ﴿al-khisam﴾ (contention) there are two interpretations:

The first: in argument.

The second: in disputation.

﴿Not clear﴾ has three interpretations:

The first: that it refers to lack of eloquence. This is related from al-Suddi.

The second: weakness of argument. Qatadah said: No woman has argued except that she was about to speak without her argument.

The third: silence in response. This is related from al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd, and from those who claimed that it refers to the idols.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And they made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾.

Regarding His saying ﴿servants of the Most Merciful﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: He named them His servants as an honour, as He said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility﴾.

The second: it is the plural of ʻabid (worshipper).

Regarding His saying ﴿females﴾ there are two interpretations:

The first: i.e., daughters of the Most Merciful.

The second: deficient with the deficiency of daughters.

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ admits of two interpretations:

The first: their witnessing at the time of their creation.

The second: their witnessing after their creation, until they knew that they were females.

﴿Their testimony will be recorded and they will be questioned﴾, i.e., their testimony will be recorded if they bore witness, and they will be questioned about it when they are resurrected.

I shall translate this passage, which is the commentary of al-Mawardi on Surah al-Zukhruf (43), verses 26–35.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when Ibrahim said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am innocent (bara') of what you worship,"﴾ al-Bara' is a verbal noun (masdar) used in the place of an adjective. It is not made dual, plural, or feminine, so it is as if he had said, "Indeed, I am innocent (bari')."

﴿Of what you worship﴾ ﴿except He who originated me﴾. This is an exceptive clause of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), and its sense is: "But He who originated me," that is, created me. ﴿Indeed, He will guide me﴾. It has also been said that there is an elided element in it, its sense being: "Except He who originated me, from whom I do not disassociate myself. ﴿Indeed, He will guide me﴾." He said this out of trust in Allah and as a warning to his people that guidance comes from his Lord.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And He made it a word remaining among his descendants﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

The first: "There is no god but Allah." There continued to be among his offspring those who said it. This was said by Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: "That you worship none but Allah." This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third: Islam, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿He named you Muslims before this﴾. This was said by Ikrimah.

As for ﴿among his descendants (aqib)﴾, there are three interpretations:

The first: his son. This was said by Ikrimah.

The second: the family of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: those who come after him. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

(p-223) ﴿So that they may return﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations:

The first: they return to the truth. This was said by Ibrahim.

The second: they repent. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: they remember. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: they return to your religion, which is the religion of Ibrahim. This was said by al-Farra'.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man of the two cities?"﴾ As for the two cities, one is Makkah and the other is al-Ta'if.

As for the great man of Makkah, there are two opinions:

One: that he is al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: 'Utbah ibn Rabi'ah. This was said by Mujahid.

As for the great man of al-Ta'if, there are four opinions:

The first: that he is Habib ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: [Umayr] ibn 'Abd Yalil, [al-Thaqafi]. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: 'Urwah ibn Mas'ud. This was said by Qatadah.

The fourth: that he is Kinanah [Abd] ibn 'Amr. This was said by al-Suddi.

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ That is, prophethood, so that they place it wherever they wish.

﴿It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾. That is, their provisions. Qatadah said: so the one who is weak in strength, little in resource, and impaired in speech, while he is given abundance, meets one who is strong in resource, eloquent in speech, while he is restricted in provision.

﴿And We have raised some of them above others in degrees﴾. Concerning it there are five interpretations:

The first: by virtues, so some are superior and some are inferior. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: by freedom and slavery, so some are owners and some are owned.

The third: by wealth and poverty, so some are rich and some are poor.

The fourth: by commanding good and forbidding evil. (p-224)

The fifth: said by al-Suddi, the preference in provision: Allah the Exalted apportioned His mercy in prophethood just as He apportioned provision in livelihood.

﴿That they may take one another in service (sukhriyyan)﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations:

One: it means servants. This was said by al-Suddi.

The second: it means possession. This was said by Qatadah.

﴿And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations:

The first: that prophethood is better than wealth.

The second: that Paradise is better than this world.

The third: that completing the obligatory duties is better than abundance of voluntary acts.

The fourth: that what He bestows upon them is better than what He rewards them for their deeds. This was said by some of the people of inspiration (ashab al-khawatir).

The saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations:

One: upon one religion, in disbelief. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: upon preferring this world over religion. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful roofs of silver for their houses﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions:

One: that they are the upper parts of the houses. This was said by Qatadah and Mujahid.

The second: the doors. This was said by al-Naqqash.

﴿And stairways upon which they would ascend﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: al-ma'arij are the stairs, which is the view of the majority; its singular is mi'raj.

﴿Upon which they would ascend (yazharun)﴾. That is, stairs of silver upon which they would climb, and al-zuhur means ascending.

It is related that Nabigha of Banu Ja'dah recited to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) his verse:

"We ascended the heavens in chastity and nobility, and indeed we hope for a station (mazhar) beyond that."

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) became angry and said: "Where to?" He said: "To Paradise." He said: "Indeed, if Allah wills."

Al-Hasan said: By Allah, the world has inclined toward most of its people, and He did not do this; so how would it be if He did?

﴿And ornament (zukhrufan)﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions:

One: that it is gold. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Qutrub recited the saying of Dhu al-Isba':

"Ornaments resembling, whose arrival you would think are sparks of fire blazing from a flame."

The second: furnishings and household goods. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that it is decorative carvings. This was said by al-Hasan.

The Almighty's words: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ have three possible meanings:

First: he turns away (yu'ridu). Qatadah said this.

*A fine young man, you walk toward the light of his fire*
*When the wind blows and the land is barren.*

Regarding His words ﴿from the remembrance of the Most Merciful﴾ there are three meanings:

First: from the remembrance of God. Qatadah said this.

Second: from what God has made clear of the lawful and the unlawful, of command and prohibition. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement.

Third: from the Qur'an, because it is the speech of the Most Merciful. al-Kalbi said this.

﴿We appoint for him a devil﴾ has two meanings:

First: We place him as a devil.

Second: We exchange for him a devil, derived from al-muqayadah (exchange), which is mutual exchange.

﴿So he is to him a companion﴾ has two statements:

First: he is a devil who is assigned to him in this world. He prevents him from what is lawful, drives him toward what is unlawful, forbids him from obedience and commands him to disobedience. This is the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's statement.

Second: when the disbeliever is raised from his grave on the Day of Resurrection, a devil is chained to his hand, and it does not leave him until both are brought by God to the Fire. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this.

The Almighty's words: ﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾ Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read it in the singular, meaning the son of Adam. The rest read *jā'ānā* in the dual, meaning the son of Adam and his companion.

﴿He will say, "Oh, I wish there were between me and you the distance of two easts"﴾ This is the statement of the son of Adam to his companion. Regarding "the two easts" there are two statements:

First: it refers to the east and the west, and one was given precedence over the other, as it is said *sunnat al-'Umarayn* (the practice of the two 'Umars). This is like the poet's saying:

*We took the horizons of the sky over you,*
*and for us are its moon and its rising stars.*

Second: it refers to the east of winter and the east of summer, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verse 51–56:

Allah's words: ﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed among his people﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

First: that "proclaimed" means "said." This was stated by Abu Malik.

Second: that he commanded someone to proclaim among his people. This was stated by Ibn Jurayj.

﴿He said, "O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me?"﴾ Regarding this there are two views:

First: that it refers to Alexandria. This was stated by Mujahid.

Second: that he ruled from it forty farsakhs in its extent. This was related by al-Naqqash.

(p-230) ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

First: there were gardens and rivers flowing beneath his palace. This was stated by Qatadah.
It is also said: beneath his throne.

Second: he meant the Nile, flowing beneath me, that is, below me.

Third: the meaning of his words ﴿And these rivers flow beneath me﴾ is that the commanders and the tyrants march beneath my banner. This was stated by al-Dahhak.

It may also allow a fourth interpretation: that by "the rivers" he meant wealth, and he expressed it by "rivers" because of its abundance and visibility. His words ﴿flow beneath me﴾ mean: I distribute it among those who follow me, because the inducement and the power lie in wealth, as in rivers.

﴿Will you not then see?﴾ This may carry two meanings:

First: Will you not see my strength and the weakness of Musa?

Second: My power to benefit you and the incapacity of Musa.

Then he openly stated his own condition, saying ﴿Am I not better﴾. al-Suddi said: "Rather, I am better."

﴿than this one who is contemptible﴾. Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: that is, weak. This was stated by Qatadah.

Second: insignificant. This was stated by Sufyan.

Third: because he used to demean himself in his own needs. This was related by Ibn Isa.

﴿and who can hardly express himself clearly﴾, that is, who cannot make himself understood. Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: that is, he is unable to speak fluently. This was stated by Qatadah.

Second: he has a lisp. This was stated by al-Zajjaj.

Third: he has a heavy tongue because of an ember he put in his mouth while he was young. This was stated by Sufyan.

Allah's words: ﴿Why have bracelets of gold not been put upon him?﴾ Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: he said this because it was the custom of the time and the dress of people of nobility.

Second: so that this would be a sign of his truthfulness. The word "asawir" is the plural of "uswira," and "uswira" is the plural of "siwar."

(p-231) ﴿Or the angels came with him in succession﴾. Regarding this there are three meanings:

First: successive, one after another. This was stated by Qatadah.

Second: they accompany one another in assistance. This was stated by al-Suddi.

Third: "muqtarinin," that is, they walk together. This was stated by Mujahid.

Regarding their coming with him there are two views:

First: so that they would be helpers for him. This was stated by Muqatil.

Second: so that they would be a proof of his truthfulness. This was stated by al-Kalbi.

But this does not necessarily follow, because the miracle is sufficient; and it was possible that he would be denied even with the coming of the angels, just as he is denied in spite of the manifest signs.

Pharaoh mentioned the angels as a report of Musa's own words, because one who does not know his Creator will not believe in the angels.

Allah's words: ﴿So he made light of his people, and they obeyed him﴾. Regarding this there are four meanings:

First: he incited them with words, and they obeyed him in denying. This was stated by Ibn Ziyad.

Second: he moved them with desire, so they hastened with him in responding. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Farra'.

Third: he made them foolish, and they displayed the obedience of their ignorance. This is the meaning of the statement of al-Kalbi.

Fourth: he called them to his falsehood, and they hastened in answering him. This was stated by Ibn Isa.

Allah's words: ﴿So when they angered Us, We took vengeance upon them﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: "they angered Us" (aghdabuna). This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

Second: "they provoked Our displeasure" (askhatuna). This was related by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

Their meanings differ, and the difference between them is that "sakhat" is the showing of dislike, while "ghadab" is the will to take revenge.

"Asaf" is grief over what has been lost.

Regarding it there are two meanings:

First: since it is placed here in the position of anger, it is correct to attribute it to Allah, because one may become angry with one who disobeys him.

(p-232) Second: that "asaf" refers to the prophets, because nothing escapes Allah the Exalted; and its implied meaning is: "When they grieved Our messengers, We took vengeance upon them."

Allah's words: ﴿So We made them a precedent﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the sin and the lam, and regarding this there are two interpretations:

First: diverse desires. This was stated by Ibn Abbas.

Second: the plural of "salaf," that is, all of those among the people who have passed away. This was stated by Ibn Isa.

The rest read it with a fatha on the sin and the lam, meaning "those who went before," and regarding this there are three meanings:

First: a precedent in the Fire. This was stated by Qatadah.

Second: a precedent for the disbelievers of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). This was stated by Mujahid.

Third: a precedent for the likes of those who did as they did. This was stated by Abu Mijlaz.

﴿and an example for the later generations﴾. Regarding this there are two meanings:

First: a lesson for others. This was stated by Qatadah.

Second: a lesson for those who come after them. This was stated by Mujahid.

The Word of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾, to the end of the verse.

On this verse there are four opinions:

The first is what Ibn 'Abbas narrated: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O assembly of Quraysh, there is no one worshipped besides Allah in whom there is any good." They said: "Do you not claim that 'Isa was a prophet and a righteous servant? Yet he was worshipped besides Allah." So this verse was revealed.

The second is what Mujahid related: that Quraysh said, "Muhammad wants us to worship him as the people of 'Isa worshipped 'Isa." So this verse was revealed.

The third is what Qatada related: that when Allah mentioned the descent of 'Isa in the Qur'an, Quraysh said, "O Muhammad, what do you intend by mentioning 'Isa?" So this verse was revealed.

Third: you shall enjoy comfort. This was said by Qatada, and comfort is in the body.

Fourth: you shall be made glad. This was said by Mujahid, and gladness is in the eye.

Umayya said to him: "My face is forbidden to your face unless you go to Muhammad and spit in his face." Uqba did so. The Prophet (ﷺ) then vowed to kill him. He killed him on the day of Badr by sabr (having him bound and killed in cold blood after capture), and he killed Umayya in the battle. The verse was revealed concerning these two.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You and your spouses, you shall be delighted﴾. There are three opinions concerning it:

First: they and their wives who were believers in this world.

Second: and those whom they are given in marriage among the houris in the Hereafter.

Third: they and their companions in this world.

Concerning ﴿tuhbarun﴾ (you shall be delighted) there are six interpretations:

First: you shall be honored. This was said by Ibn Abbas, and honor is in rank.

Second: you shall rejoice. This was said by al-Hasan, and joy is in the heart.

Third: you shall enjoy comfort. This was said by Qatada, and comfort is in the body.

Fourth: you shall be made glad. This was said by Mujahid, and gladness is in the eye.

Fifth: you shall be amazed. This was said by Ibn Abi Najih, and amazement here means perceiving what is rare and wondrous.

Sixth: that it is the enjoyment of hearing. This was said by Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and cups﴾ (wa-akwab). There are five opinions concerning it:

First: that it means vessels with round mouths. This was said by Mujahid.

Second: that they have no handles. This was said by al-Suddi.

Third: that the kub is the round one with a short neck and short handle, while the ibriq is the one with a long neck and long handle. This was said by Qatada.

Fourth: that they are ewers (abariq) without spouts. This was said by al-Akhfash.

Fifth: that they are ewers without handles. This was said by Qutrub.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And therein is what the souls desire and what the eyes delight in﴾. Nafi', Ibn Amir, and Asim in the transmission of Hafs read ﴿tashtahīhi﴾ (the souls desire it, with the pronoun attached). Two meanings are possible:

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verses 74–80:

The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik (the keeper of Hell)!"﴾ This is the call of the people of the Fire to its guardians when they have tasted its punishment.

﴿Let your Lord put an end to us.﴾ That is, let Him cause us to die. They sought death so that they might find rest from the punishment of the Fire.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ That is, you will remain in its punishment, alive. Regarding the length of time between their call and the reply, there are four opinions:

The first: forty years. This was said by Abdullah ibn Amr.

The second: eighty years. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: one hundred years. This was said by Nawf.

(p-240) The fourth: one thousand years. This was said by Ibn Abbas, because the greater the gap between the call and the answer, the more humiliating and degrading it is for them.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or have they determined a matter? Then indeed, We are determining a matter.﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: "Or have they agreed upon denial? Then indeed, We are agreed upon requiting them with resurrection." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "Or have they devised a plot? Then indeed, We are devising a plot against them." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: "They have decided a matter, so indeed, We are decreeing against them the punishment." This was said by al-Kalbi.

It has also been said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh when their leaders gathered in Dar al-Nadwah (the Assembly House) to consult about the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), until their opinion settled on what Abu Jahl had suggested to them: that one man from each tribe should come forward so that they would all share in killing him, and thus the demand for his blood would be weakened. Then this verse was revealed, and Allah destroyed all of them, upon them be the curse, on the Day of Badr.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verses 74–80:

The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And they will call, "O Malik (the keeper of Hell)!"﴾ This is the call of the people of the Fire to its guardians when they have tasted its punishment.

﴿Let your Lord put an end to us.﴾ That is, let Him cause us to die. They sought death so that they might find rest from the punishment of the Fire.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will remain."﴾ That is, you will remain in its punishment, alive. Regarding the length of time between their call and the reply, there are four opinions:

The first: forty years. This was said by Abdullah ibn Amr.

The second: eighty years. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: one hundred years. This was said by Nawf.

(p-240) The fourth: one thousand years. This was said by Ibn Abbas, because the greater the gap between the call and the answer, the more humiliating and degrading it is for them.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Or have they determined a matter? Then indeed, We are determining a matter.﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations:

The first: "Or have they agreed upon denial? Then indeed, We are agreed upon requiting them with resurrection." This was said by Qatadah.

The second: "Or have they devised a plot? Then indeed, We are devising a plot against them." This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: "They have decided a matter, so indeed, We are decreeing against them the punishment." This was said by al-Kalbi.

It has also been said that this verse was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Quraysh when their leaders gathered in Dar al-Nadwah (the Assembly House) to consult about the matter of the Prophet (ﷺ), until their opinion settled on what Abu Jahl had suggested to them: that one man from each tribe should come forward so that they would all share in killing him, and thus the demand for his blood would be weakened. Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 43, verse 81–89:

First: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first to worship Allah, Who has no son." This was said by Ibn Zayd and Mujahid.

Second: Its meaning is "then I would be the first of the worshippers, but there is not, and it is not fitting that there should be." This was said by Qatadah.

Third: "Say: the Most Merciful has not had a son, and I am the first of the witnesses that He has no son." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

Fourth: "Say: the Most Merciful did not have a son." This is a complete sentence, and then he resumed: "then I am the first of the worshippers," i.e., the monotheists among the people of Makkah. This was said by al-Suddi.

Fifth: "Say: If you claim that the Most Merciful has a son, then I am the first of those who deny that He has a son." This was said by Sufyan.

Sixth: "If the Most Merciful had a son, then I would be the first of those who are disdainful (ánifin) that He should have a son." This was said by al-Kisa'i and Ibn Qutaybah, and from it is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Those are my fathers, so bring me the likes of them, and I refuse to satirize Tamim with Darim."

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And He is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth.﴾ This is a refutation that anything other than Allah could be a god, and that the God is the One who is God in the heaven and God on the earth; and this attribute does not belong to anyone other than Allah, so it is necessary that He be the God.

In the meaning of the statement there are two aspects:

One: that He is the One who is unique in the heaven and the earth. This was said by Muqatil.

The second: that He is the One who is worshipped in the heaven and the earth. This was said by al-Kalbi.

﴿And He is the All-Wise, the All-Knowing.﴾ This may have two aspects:

One: that He mentions this as an attribute to exalt Him.

The second: that He mentions it as a reason for His divinity, because He is All-Wise and All-Knowing, and there is no All-Wise and All-Knowing among the idols.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Him have no power of intercession.﴾ On it there are two opinions:

One: "Shirkah" (partnership), and from it comes "shufʿah" (pre-emption) in sale, due to the partner's entitlement to it.

The meaning of the statement would be that those who are called upon besides Allah do not possess a partnership with Allah by which they would deserve to be gods, except that they bear witness before Allah to the truth concerning one who has a right over them or who has a right. This is the meaning of the statement of Ibn Bahr.

The second: that intercession (al-shafa'ah) is the seeking of compassion from the one interceded with regarding what is hoped for, and the seeking of pardon from him regarding what is feared. This is the view of the majority.

It has been said that the occasion of its revelation was what is related: that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and a group of Quraysh said, "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will take the angels as protectors, and they are more worthy of intercession for us than he is." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed: ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Him have no power of intercession﴾, meaning those whom they worship besides Allah, who are the angels, [have no power of] intercession for them.

Qatadah said: they are the angels, Jesus and Uzair, because they were worshipped besides Allah.

﴿Except those who bear witness to the truth while they know.﴾ On it there are two aspects:

One: meaning that the testimony to the truth is only for those who bore witness to the truth in the world while they knew that it is the truth, so the angels intercede for them. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: that the angels intercede only for one who testified that there is no god but Allah while they knew that Allah is their Lord.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿And [He has] knowledge of his saying: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."﴾ It is recited in three ways: with the accusative, the genitive and the nominative.

As for the genitive, it is the reading of ʿĀsim and Hamzah, and in meaning it refers back to His statement, ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, and the knowledge of his saying.

As for the nominative, it is the reading of al-Aʿraj, and its meaning is an inception (ibtidaʾ), and "his saying" (qīlahu): it is said that it is Muhammad: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."

Al-qīl is al-qawl (the saying).

As for the accusative, it is the reading of the rest of the leading reciters, and in its interpretation there are four aspects:

One: with the meaning of "except those who bore witness to the truth and said his saying, 'My Lord, these are a people who do not believe,'" in the form of denouncing them. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: that it means "or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk, and his saying, 'My Lord'?" This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: with the meaning of "and Muhammad complained to his Lord of his saying," then a new beginning, which informs: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿So turn away from them.﴾ Qatadah said: He commanded him to pardon them, then He commanded him to fight them, so the pardoning became abrogated by the sword.

It may also mean pardoning their foolishness, by not responding to them in kind, as a recommendation to him toward forbearance.

﴿And say, "Peace."﴾ On it there are five aspects:

One: meaning, say that by which you are safe from their evil. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: say good in exchange for their evil; said by al-Suddi.

The third: meaning, forbear toward them; said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that He commanded him to bid them farewell with peace, and did not make it a greeting to them; related by al-Naqqash.

The fifth: that He taught him by this how to give peace to them; related by Shu'ayb ibn al-Hubab.

﴿But they will come to know.﴾ It may carry two matters:

One: they will come to know the descent of punishment upon them.

The second: they will come to know the truthfulness of your warning them, and Allah knows best.

As for the genitive, it is the reading of ʿĀsim and Hamzah, and in meaning it refers back to His statement, ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾, and the knowledge of his saying.

As for the nominative, it is the reading of al-Aʿraj, and its meaning is an inception (ibtidaʾ), and "his saying" (qīlahu): it is said that it is Muhammad: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe."

Al-qīl is al-qawl (the saying).

As for the accusative, it is the reading of the rest of the leading reciters, and in its interpretation there are four aspects:

One: with the meaning of "except those who bore witness to the truth and said his saying, 'My Lord, these are a people who do not believe,'" in the form of denouncing them. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: that it means "or do they think that We do not hear their secret and their private talk, and his saying, 'My Lord'?" This was said by Yahya ibn Salam.

The third: with the meaning of "and Muhammad complained to his Lord of his saying," then a new beginning, which informs: "My Lord, these are a people who do not believe." This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The Exalted's statement: ﴿So turn away from them.﴾ Qatadah said: He commanded him to pardon them, then He commanded him to fight them, so the pardoning became abrogated by the sword.

It may also mean pardoning their foolishness, by not responding to them in kind, as a recommendation to him toward forbearance.

﴿And say, "Peace."﴾ On it there are five aspects:

One: meaning, say that by which you are safe from their evil. This was said by Ibn ʿIsa.

The second: say good in exchange for their evil; said by al-Suddi.

The third: meaning, forbear toward them; said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: that He commanded him to bid them farewell with peace, and did not make it a greeting to them; related by al-Naqqash.

The fifth: that He taught him by this how to give peace to them; related by Shu'ayb ibn al-Hubab.

﴿But they will come to know.﴾ It may carry two matters:

One: they will come to know the descent of punishment upon them.

The second: they will come to know the truthfulness of your warning them, and Allah knows best.
